extraction.name: 94% on CIFAR-10 in 3.29 Seconds on a Single GPU
extraction.description: The paper introduces training methods for CIFAR-10 that reach 94% accuracy in 3.29 seconds, 95% in 10.4 seconds, and 96% in 46.3 seconds on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, and proposes a derandomized horizontal flipping augmentation called alternating flip.
extraction.creator: Keller Jordan
extraction.citeAs: Keller Jordan. 94% on CIFAR-10 in 3.29 Seconds on a Single GPU. arXiv:2404.00498v2, 2024.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The work uses the CIFAR-10 dataset, described as containing 60,000 32x32 color images labeled as one of ten classes, divided into a training set of 50,000 images and a validation set of 10,000 images. In the released code, the data are loaded via torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10 with download=True and saved locally as train.pt and test.pt.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data are CIFAR-10 images and labels loaded from torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10; the code saves images, labels, and classes from the dataset.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The training pipeline applies horizontal flipping augmentation, 2-pixel random translation implemented as reflection padding followed by a random 32x32 crop, and for the 96% target adds 12-pixel Cutout augmentation. The paper also proposes alternating flip, where images are randomly flipped in the first epoch and then deterministically alternated across subsequent epochs. During evaluation, test-time augmentation uses horizontal flipping and two extra crops, producing six augmented views per test image whose outputs are combined by weighted averaging.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: In the released code, images are converted from uint8 to half precision, scaled by dividing by 255, permuted to channel-first format, and normalized using CIFAR mean and standard deviation. For training, images may be pre-padded with reflection padding for translation augmentation, randomly cropped, and flipped. The first convolution is initialized using patch-whitening statistics computed from 2x2 patches of normalized training images.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset consists of images each labeled as one of ten classes; the paper uses the existing CIFAR-10 labels and does not describe creating new annotations.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The code is released at https://github.com/KellerJordan/cifar10-airbench and as the airbench Python package. No updating timeframe, maintainers, or deprecation policy are specified.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that faster CIFAR-10 training can accelerate research, reduce the cost of experiments, decrease the cost of projects involving massive numbers of trained networks, and make it possible to replicate large-scale studies with fewer computational resources.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The methods were developed solely to maximize training speed on CIFAR-10. The compiled version has a one-time compilation cost of up to several minutes and is only beneficial when many runs are executed. The paper notes that some comparisons are situational, for example airbench96 uses test-time augmentation whereas standard ResNet-18 training does not. No explicit dataset bias analysis is provided.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is used for training and evaluation of image classification models on CIFAR-10, with the paper specifically targeting fast training to 94%, 95%, and 96% accuracy. The methods are intended to accelerate experimental iteration, support large numbers of training runs, and enable hyperparameter comparisons. The paper also evaluates generalization to CIFAR-100, SVHN, CINIC-10, and ImageNet settings.
